chapter_theme: Under the heading ஒழுக்கம், nine verses on keeping one's own conduct: conduct as richness added to good birth, taking a good word from any mouth, walking by one's own way, the limits of advice to the fixed, mending one's own faults before others', choosing ruin before a lasting scar, curing undeserved reproach, the shameless untouched by blame, and the evil tongue that spares no one.

34.reading: For those of excellent descent who come shining from an old line to live as men of conduct is, the verse asks the lord of the watered town where ripe coconuts drop into the fields, like rich milk with ghee on it poured out.
34.nuance: The verse treats old lineage as a good in its own right and good conduct as what is added on top of it, abundance upon abundance, as the ripe coconut falling into the paddy field doubles a fertile land. The proverb is hard: நெய்த்தலைப்பால் உக்கு விடல் could also be read as a waste (spilling the cream-topped milk), but that sits ill with the praise in lines 1-2; the reading takes it as richness overflowing.

pazhamozhi.literal: milk with ghee on its top, poured out

story.act: no story; the proverb stands for richness added to richness

pazhamozhi.applied_to: good conduct in the well-born adds excellence to an excellence already given by birth

35.reading: As fragrant agil comes from the kalli and an omen from the black crow's call, one should not scorn a good word from whatever mouth it comes, says the verse to the lord of the hill country of loud clear falls, for if a dog has caught a monitor lizard even brahmins eat it.
35.nuance: The two opening images are low sources of something prized: a scented wood from a thorny spurge and a meaningful sign from a despised bird. The proverb takes the extreme case: பார்ப்பார், the brahmins, a birth-group named here for its strict abstention from flesh, will eat what a dog (itself an impure catcher) has brought in, if it is good. The caste term is not used to rank people but to set the hardest test of a rule against a low source.

norm.note: the proverb presumes the period's norm that brahmins abstain from flesh and shun what a dog has touched, and makes its breaking the measure of a good thing's pull

pazhamozhi.literal: if a dog catches a monitor lizard, even brahmins eat it

story.act: no story; a type case in which the lowness of the bringer does not stop even the strictest eater

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a good word is to be taken whatever the lowness of the mouth that speaks it

36.reading: The verse tells its hearer, addressed as அத்தா, not to become like the small men who do not watch their own conduct, do not know the way their kin came and never join the straight path, but to walk by his own conduct, since no one knows that conduct apart from him.
36.nuance: The proverb can be taken two ways: that only the man himself knows his own conduct, so he must be its keeper, or that others know a man's conduct only from the man himself, so he is its evidence. Both make conduct a thing the self answers for, against the small men who look neither at themselves nor at their forebears.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who can know your walk apart from you

story.act: no story; the proverb is said to the hearer himself

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man must keep his own conduct because it is known only through him

37.reading: When someone takes up a course that is not fit and off the path, turning him back and setting him right is beyond even the great, even those of keen and subtle learning and wisdom, for a drum sounds what has been set in it.
37.nuance: The verse puts the limit not in the adviser but in the advised: learning and hearing (கூர்த்தநுண் கேள்வி) do not reach one who has chosen. The proverb's ஓர்த்தது is what has been resolved or intended; the drum gives back only that, as a fixed man gives back only his resolve.

pazhamozhi.literal: a drum sounds what it has been set to

story.act: no story; the drum stands for the man fixed on his own purpose

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a man set on a wrong course cannot be turned back even by the wisest

38.reading: To push in anywhere to remove others' faults without removing one's own is, in all the wide world, the goat that clears another's wind and not its own.
38.nuance: The verse's words தங்குற்றம் நீக்கல and பிறர்குற்றம் are the Kural's own pair (436), turned from a condition of the king's justice into a mockery of any meddler. The proverb's goat is a curer that cannot cure itself; வளி is the wind-disorder of the body.

pazhamozhi.proverb: வெள்ளாடு தன்வளி தீராது அயல்வளி தீர்த்து விடல்
pazhamozhi.literal: the goat does not clear its own wind but clears its neighbour's

story.act: no story; the goat is any healer of others who leaves his own sickness

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who corrects others' faults while keeping his own is absurd

39.reading: Even when one is told 'I will be ruined', one must do only what brings no scar on oneself, for in the land ringed by the full sea and its long hills, a stone wears away but a word does not.
39.nuance: கெடுவல் is the man's own ruin, which the verse accepts as the lesser loss; the scar (வடு) is the reproach a deed leaves, and the proverb's word is what is said of the doer, which outlives the hills.

pazhamozhi.literal: stone wears away, a word does not

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the lasting word against the wearing stone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one should choose ruin over a shameful deed, since the report of it lasts

40.reading: For the evil disease called unfitting reproach, the medicine is excellence of character, and if it is not cured by medicine, says the verse to the lord of the cool sea shore, the disease destroys one's strength.
40.nuance: பொருந்தாப் பழி is most likely blame that does not fit the man, an undeserved reproach, though it may be reproach that should never attach to him; either way the verse does not tell him to ignore it but to answer it with மாட்சி, as a disease must be treated or it wastes the body.

story.act: no story; untreated illness stands for untreated reproach

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a reproach must be answered by worth of conduct or it ruins the man

41.reading: Even the nerunji thorn can do nothing to hurt the inner soles of those who walk with scraping feet, says the verse to the lord of the cool shore of beating waves where the serunthi bends over the wide backwater, and even great reproach is nothing to those who do not care for it.
41.nuance: The verse is not praise of indifference: the hardened sole stands for the shameless, whom blame cannot reach as it reaches the man who cares. Under the heading ஒழுக்கம் it describes a failure, not a strength.

pazhamozhi.literal: even great reproach does not exist for those who do not mind it

story.act: no story; the proverb names a type, the man who does not heed blame

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the shameless are untouched by reproach as calloused feet by thorns

42.reading: The world calls even Mal, the lord who bore the hard cold rain for the cows, a mere cowherd, and there is no need to ask whether it is gods or men: the tongue that speaks evil never runs short.
42.nuance: The parse takes மாலையும் as மால் with உம் (even Mal) rather than மாலை, evening, and கோவிற்கு as 'to the lord'. On that reading the example is a god whose saving act is turned into a slight on his rank; the point is that slander spares no one.

pazhamozhi.literal: the tongue that speaks evil knows no poverty

story.act: Mal, having sheltered the cows from hard cold rain, is still called by the world a cowherd
story.tradition: by tradition the Govardhana episode, in which Krishna holds up the hill against the rain for the cattle; the verse names only the sheltering of the cows

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the evil-speaking tongue finds something to belittle even in a god's saving deed

links.note: Kural 133 makes conduct itself the substance of noble birth and its lapse low birth; Pazhamozhi 34 keeps old lineage as a good already held and makes conduct an addition upon it.
links.teaches: Read together they show two models of lineage: in the Kural birth is earned by conduct, in Pazhamozhi conduct enriches a birth already counted as excellent.
links.list_adds: its proverb of milk upon ghee makes conduct a second richness laid on lineage, a layering the couplet's identity of the two removes.

links.note: Naladiyar 195 says good and bad lineage are words with nothing behind them; Pazhamozhi 34 treats excellent descent from an old line as a real distinction. The conflict holds on reading 34's விழுத்தொடையர் and தொல் வந்தார் as birth.
links.teaches: The pair shows the ethics group divided on whether lineage is a fact before conduct: the Jain quatrain empties the word, the proverb collection banks on it.
links.list_adds: its abundance image treats birth and conduct as two goods to be summed, where the quatrain allows only austerity, learning and effort to make a line.

links.note: Kural 423 says wisdom is seeing the true substance of what is heard from whatever mouth; Pazhamozhi 35 forbids scorning a good word from whatever mouth and proves it by low sources of prized things.
links.teaches: The Kural states the indifference to the speaker as a test of wisdom; Pazhamozhi shows its price, even the strictest abstainer taking what a dog has caught.
links.list_adds: it gives three low sources of good things, the spurge, the crow and the dog, and ends on a breach of a birth-group's diet as the extreme case.

links.note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; Pazhamozhi 36 tells the hearer not to be like the small and to walk by his own conduct, which none knows apart from him.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the touchstone; Pazhamozhi places it inside the man, so the one who must test the deeds first is the doer.
links.list_adds: it sets the small man's three failures (not watching himself, not knowing his forebears, not joining the right path) before turning the touchstone on the hearer.

links.note: Kural 849 says one who shows things to the unseeing becomes unseeing himself while the other keeps what he saw; Pazhamozhi 37 says even the subtly learned cannot turn back one who has taken a wrong course.
links.teaches: The Kural mocks the would-be teacher; Pazhamozhi removes the blame from him, since even the wisest fail when the pupil's resolve is fixed like a drum's sound.
links.list_adds: it raises the adviser to the great and the keenly learned to show the failure is not his, and its drum gives the cause: a mind sounds only what it has resolved.

links.note: Kural 436 says a ruler who removes his own fault and then sees others' has no fault; Pazhamozhi 38 uses the same pair of own fault and others' fault to mock anyone who corrects others first.
links.teaches: Held together, the Kural's condition for a king's just correction becomes in Pazhamozhi a rule for anyone, and the reversed order is made ridiculous rather than unjust.
links.list_adds: it carries the king's condition into common life and adds the goat that cures others' wind and not its own, turning a rule into a jest.

links.note: Kural 656 forbids a deed the worthy condemn even to feed one's starving mother; Pazhamozhi 39 forbids a scarring deed even to save oneself from ruin.
links.teaches: The Kural tests the rule against duty to another, Pazhamozhi against self-preservation, and gives the reason both leave out: the word about the deed outlasts stone.
links.list_adds: its proverb supplies the reason behind the refusal, the lasting report, which the couplet leaves as a bare command.

links.note: Kural 129 says the scar (வடு) burned by the tongue never heals; Pazhamozhi 39 says one must do nothing that leaves a scar (வடு) on oneself, since a word does not wear away.
links.teaches: The pair turns the tongue's unhealing scar both ways: the Kural's falls on the one spoken to, Pazhamozhi's on the one spoken of, and both last for the same reason.
links.list_adds: it moves the scar from the wound of harsh speech to the reproach a deed earns, and sets it against stone for duration.

links.note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a flame in a lamp; Pazhamozhi 40 says undeserved reproach is a disease that, untreated by excellence of character, destroys a man.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar makes the pure immune to slander; Pazhamozhi denies immunity and asks for treatment, so worth must act against blame rather than merely survive it.
links.list_adds: its medical frame of disease, medicine and wasting gives reproach a course and a cure, where the quatrain gives only the steady flame.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 40 makes reproach a disease that wastes the man it strikes; 41 says great reproach does not exist for those who do not heed it.
links.teaches: Together they show that blame wounds only those who care for their name, so the disease of verse 40 is itself a mark of the man worth curing.

links.note: Naladiyar 189 sets the pure heart unshaken against cruel slander; Pazhamozhi 42 says the evil tongue never runs short and spares not even a god.
links.teaches: Pazhamozhi shows how far slander reaches, even to Mal's saving act, which is why the Naladiyar's steadiness must hold against slander that cannot be avoided.
links.list_adds: its example of a god called a cowherd shows slander turning a saving act into a slight on rank, a case beyond the quatrain's general slanderer.
